To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

post-tenure reviews have been implemented at 60 percent of graduate institutions and 50 percent of undergraduate institutions in the United States; they were instituted primarily in response to the rhetoric surrounding the "accountability" movement; they were implemented with the intent to improve teaching and research; they were implemented in a manner consistent with their stated intent; and they are perceived by faculty as having a positive impact on the teaching and research of their colleagues.

(1) post-tenure reviews have been adopted by only a few institutions; (2) the reviews that do exist have not been widely publicized or widely known; (3) most reviews do not include any form of evaluation of faculty performance; (4) most reviews are not used to make personnel decisions; and (5) most reviews are conducted in a manner that is consistent with the traditional tenure process

(1) post-tenure reviews are being conducted in the majority of U.S. graduate schools; (2) the vast majority of graduate institutions are not conducting post-tenure peer reviews; (3) the vast majority (80 percent) of institutions that are conducting post-tenute reviews are using a peer review process; and (4) most graduate institutions that conduct post-tenure evaluations do so in a manner that is consistent with the AAUP's "Redbook" recommendations
In summary, our research is concerned with
the perceptions of chief executive officers and faculty representatives regarding post-tenue review policy and practice at graduate institutions in the United States.
the following questions: (1) What are the perceptions of graduate institutions regarding the purposes of post-tenure reviews? (2) What are the perceived benefits and costs of post-tenute reviews?
the question: What is the nature of post-tenure reviews and how do they affect the faculty?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the post-tenure practices of the majority of graduate institutions in the United States do not appear to have a major impact on faculty status, and that the practices do not have a major impact either on institutional governance, or on the quality of graduate education and research.
the post-tenure reviews at U.S. institutions are not a serious attempt to improve the performance of the faculty.
the survey results suggest that post-tenure practices have been more symbolic than substantive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the majority of institutions that have post-tenure reviews have done little to implement them.
post-tenure reviews are more likely to be symbolic than substantive.
the current state of post-tenure practices is not a positive one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
post-tenure reviews are not a panacea for the problems of faculty accountability.
the rhetoric and practice of post-tenure evaluation are not aligned.
the post-tenure reviews that are in practice at graduate institutions are not the reviews that were intended by the policy.
